title: No quick fixes for the squeeze on refined products
gist: Roughly 5 million b/d of global refining capacity is offline after Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and the Strait of Hormuz crisis, pushing US diesel cracks to an all-time high of $100 per barrel and average US diesel to $5.65 per gallon. With US refinery utilization already at 98 percent and distillate stocks at a seasonal record low of 103.4 million barrels, there is no near-term policy fix, and product prices should stay elevated even through the weak fall shoulder season.

insights.claim: About 5 million barrels per day of global refining capacity is currently offline, even though global refining capacity has risen 15 percent over the past two decades.
insights.so_what: Capacity additions do not protect against outage-driven product tightness; crack spreads, not crude, are where the shock is being expressed.
insights.quote: about 5 million barrels per day (b/d) of global refining capacity is currently offline
insights.locator: The refinery factor
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: Ukrainian attacks over the past year have knocked out at least 30 percent of Russian refining capacity, driving Russian petroleum product exports to roughly 1.1 million b/d in July and August, the lowest level in twenty years.
insights.so_what: A 30 percent hit to a top-three diesel exporter is a structural, not seasonal, loss of supply — watch Turkish and Mediterranean import reroutes for the marginal price setter.
insights.quote: Ukrainian attacks in the past year have knocked out at least 30 percent of Russian refining capacity.
insights.locator: The largest hit to refined products
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: Russia has banned gasoline exports through January 2027 and diesel exports until at least September 30, with the diesel ban likely to be extended, forcing its usual buyers in Turkey and the Mediterranean to find alternative suppliers.
insights.so_what: Export bans lock in the physical shortfall through winter — a bullish structural bid under Mediterranean and Atlantic-basin diesel differentials.
insights.locator: Russia has now banned gasoline exports
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: Shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea plus Iranian attacks on Arab Gulf refineries cut Gulf refinery production to 7.6 million b/d in Q2 2026 from 9.6 million b/d a year earlier.
insights.so_what: A 2 million b/d year-on-year Gulf refining loss is larger than the Russian hit and its duration is unknown — the single biggest swing factor for 2027 product balances.
insights.locator: The other key cause of declining product exports
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: The International Energy Agency estimates that diesel exports from Russia, the Middle East, and Asia fell by 1.3 million b/d in July versus a year earlier, with China also cutting exports during the early Strait of Hormuz crisis.
insights.so_what: Quantifies the aggregate export hole that US barrels have had to fill — the benchmark against which any Chinese quota release should be measured.
insights.locator: In yet another blow to global product supplies
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: Crude oil and refined product prices can diverge sharply, as they did in 2022 after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and as they are doing again today, so falling crude does not guarantee relief at the pump.
insights.so_what: Do not use crude futures as a proxy for the consumer fuel bill or for refiner earnings in an outage-driven regime; trade the crack, not the barrel.
insights.quote: Even if crude prices fall, product prices could remain stubbornly high in the coming months.
insights.locator: Refinery outages in Russia and the Middle East
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: The average US diesel price hit $5.65 per gallon in the week of August 24, up 52 percent year on year.
insights.so_what: A 52 percent year-on-year diesel move is a direct cost shock to freight, rail, agriculture, and any margin-thin logistics-heavy business.
insights.quote: The average US diesel price hit $5.65 per gallon the week of August 24—up 52 percent year on year.
insights.locator: Refinery outages in Russia and the Middle East
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: The NYMEX 3-2-1 crack spread has climbed to about $70 per barrel and the US diesel crack spread has hit an all-time high of $100 per barrel.
insights.so_what: An all-time-high distillate crack is the cleanest expression of this dislocation and the direct earnings driver for merchant refiners.
insights.quote: In the United States, the diesel crack spread has hit an all-time high of $100 per barrel.
insights.locator: Uneven impacts
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: Marathon Petroleum, Valero, and Phillips 66 together earned $12.6 billion in the second quarter of 2026.
insights.so_what: Names the three listed beneficiaries and puts a number on the windfall — the cash-return and buyback capacity implied is the second-order trade.
insights.locator: Marathon Petroleum, Valero, and Phillips 66
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: The shock is distributionally uneven: refiners are capturing record margins at the same time that high transportation costs are hurting truck drivers and shippers.
insights.so_what: Long refining versus short freight-cost-exposed transport and distribution is the implied pair trade in a distillate squeeze.
insights.locator: At the same time, transportation costs are running high
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: Combined US crude and petroleum product exports jumped from an annual average of 10.7 million b/d in 2025 to an all-time high of 13.3 million b/d on a four-week moving average in May 2026, which was a key factor containing global crude prices after February 28.
insights.so_what: US export elasticity has been the global shock absorber — any policy that curbs it would re-tighten world balances rather than domestic ones.
insights.locator: US product exports rise
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: US distillate fuel oil stocks fell to 103.4 million barrels in the week ending August 21, a record low for that time of year, heading into the fall and winter demand season.
insights.so_what: Record-low seasonal distillate cover means any cold snap or refinery accident translates almost immediately into price spikes — asymmetric upside risk to distillate.
insights.locator: But there is a downside to this export boom.
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: US refinery utilization has already reached as high as 98 percent, so output cannot be pushed higher without compromising safety, leaving the White House with essentially no near-term supply lever.
insights.so_what: Political pressure on refiners will not add barrels; expect rhetoric rather than supply, which keeps cracks supported.
insights.quote: refinery utilization rates have already soared to as high as 98 percent as companies aim to capitalize on strong profit margins. They cannot be pushed further without compromising safety.
insights.locator: Policy considerations
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: The greater near-term risk is that refiners defer maintenance during the traditional fall turnaround season to chase margins, so that any accident knocking out capacity would create significant additional supply problems.
insights.so_what: Deferred maintenance builds a fat tail of unplanned-outage risk into Q4 and Q1 — a reason to own upside optionality on distillate cracks.
insights.quote: the greater risk is that refiners defer maintenance during the traditional fall turnaround season
insights.locator: Indeed, the greater risk is that refiners
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: The White House convened US refiners on September 1 and produced no significant announcements, which itself demonstrated how limited very-near-term options are.
insights.so_what: Treat headline risk from Washington jawboning as noise rather than a supply catalyst.
insights.locator: The White House convened US refiners on September 1
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: The EPA ended summer blend gasoline requirements ahead of schedule and exempted some small refiners from biofuels blending requirements, but reallocating the exempted volumes into the 2026 and 2027 cycles raises the future burden on larger refiners while doing very little to boost near-term output.
insights.so_what: Watch RIN cost exposure shifting toward large refiners in 2026-27 — a margin headwind embedded in a policy sold as relief.
insights.locator: The Environmental Protection Agency had already ended summer blend
insights.speaker: srothbardt

themes.theme: Structural refining geography and inventory doctrine

insights.claim: Older, less efficient refineries have closed across Europe and the United States while newer and larger capacity has concentrated in the Middle East and China, creating two distinct energy security exposures.
insights.so_what: Product supply risk now travels with Middle East conflict and Chinese policy rather than with OECD refinery economics — reprice geographic risk premia accordingly.
insights.locator: Aside from these acute shocks, there is a longer-running supply challenge.
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: Spare global refining capacity is now concentrated in China, where the government can adjust refined product export quotas with little advance warning and without regard for regional or global product balances.
insights.so_what: Chinese quota announcements are now the single largest discretionary swing factor in global product balances — a policy headline that can move cracks instantly.
insights.quote: spare capacity in global refining is now concentrated in China, where the government can adjust refined product export quotas with little advance warning
insights.locator: This presents two energy security challenges.
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: The IEA's ninety-day stockholding obligation lets member countries choose flexibly between crude and refined product stocks and between government and commercial inventories, and the Hormuz shock argues for re-evaluating that balance or setting minimum shares for refined products.
insights.so_what: A shift toward mandated product stocks would create structural incremental demand for distillate storage and inventory — a slow-burn bullish factor for storage assets and product demand.
insights.locator: The International Energy Agency would be an appropriate venue
insights.speaker: srothbardt

insights.claim: Technical constraints on storing fuels for prolonged periods and the cost of building, maintaining, and managing storage facilities impose significant limits on any policy of holding larger refined product reserves.
insights.so_what: Products degrade and cost more to hold than crude, so a product-reserve buildout would be slow and expensive — do not expect it to cap prices in this cycle.
insights.locator: However, technical constraints on storing fuels
insights.speaker: srothbardt
